newsitem.title: UK: UK gilt auction lapped up despite looming election.
newsitem.headline: UK gilt auction lapped up despite looming election.

text.p: An auction of five-year UK gilts on Wednesday met a tidal wave of demand, scotching fears that a looming election would keep investors on the sidelines.
The Bank of England's sale of two billion pounds of 7.0 percent gilts due 2002 attracted bids worth nearly seven billion pounds, representing cover of 3.49 times.
Most dealers had forecast cover of around two times.
"There were a whole host of reasons for this stock to go well and we always thought it would," said Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW.
He said the auction stock offered the most attractive yield pick-up of any five-year government bonds in Europe.
"And there's good demand for it in the repo market too, so you can get cheap money by repoing it out as well," he added.

Earlier this week, the auction stock was trading about 15 basis points through general collateral rates on the gilt repo market. So by lending the bond out, an investor could receive money 15 basis points cheaper than the general going rate.

Adams also said most investors holding the 7.0 percent gilt due 2001 would want to roll into the 2002 at some point. "The '02 is still quite a small stock. It's dwarfed by the amount of 2001s out there."

All those factors outweighed any uncertainty thrown up by the British election, due in just eight days. Only a consistent narrowing of the opinion polls, hinting at a hung parliament in which no party holds an overall majority, would shake gilt investors' confidence, analysts said.
An opinion poll in the Guardian newspaper on Wednesday showed the opposition Labour Party's lead cut to just five percent from 14. Experts said that was probably a rogue result.

"I think the market has tended to discount that poll," said Stephen Lewis, chief economist at London Bond Broking. "We would need to see at least one or two more like that before we get really worried."

A Gallup poll, also out overnight, put Labour's lead at 21 points. Lewis pointed to the June long gilt future, up 8/32 on the day at 109-21, to show how little anxiety the market felt about Labour's lead evaporating.
Adams agreed. "The election will only become an issue if all the polls go the same way as the Guardian's did."

It may seem odd for Britain's traditionally Conservative-supporting financial markets to yearn for a clear Labour win but the last thing they want is the uncertainty of a hung parliament. The polls suggest there is no prospect of a working Tory majority.

Whatever the election result, gilt investors queued up to buy Wednesday's offering, leaving a yield tail of just one basis point. That indicates the Bank hardly had to drop its price at all to attract enough buyers.
"The yield was broadly in line with expectations. It doesn't seem there was any pressure on the market to absorb the stock," Lewis said.

Adams said the gilt market looked in good shape, assuming interest rates were put up soon after the election to counter booming domestic demand. "We saw massive curve flattening late last year. That could soon be back on the agenda."

And with the Bank of England selling nearly four billion pounds more gilts than it needed to in the last financial year, as Britain's public sector borrowing requirement undercut forecasts, supply will not be a problem either.

Don Smith, analyst at HSBC Markets, said lower supply alone would not spark a rally. "Nevertheless, the squeeze in issuance should provide a solid platform for a market rally later in the year, should other fundamentals turn bullish."
